posts.title: The Men Who Came Home – A Memorial Part Seventeen – The Surrey Regiments
posts.description: The Queen’s – The Royal West Surrey Regiment – lost 7,399 men killed during the Great War. Bill, Ernest & George were not among them, but they fought, and suffered, for their country, just the same. They just aren’t remembered as the men who died are. More men of the Queen’s in later life. Walter, a pre-war regular soldier, on the left, was wounded in the left leg in France on 31st October 1914. He would recover and serve throughout the remainder of the war, being discharged in March 1919 after seven and a half years’ service. He would suffer from encephalitis lethargica in the mid-1920s and be diagnosed with ‘Typical advanced Parkinsonian Syndrome; he is bedridden and totally helpless’ by the early thirties. He would hang on to life until 1940, at which time he was still under fifty years old. posts.title: The Road to Passchendaele: New Irish Farm Cemetery – Eighteen Years On
posts.description: That’s eighteen years since I last set foot in this cemetery, before you ask. And I don’t imagine it’s changed a huge amount, although you never know. At the time there was no ‘With the British Army in Flanders’ website, nor any thought of such a thing. But within a few years we were up and running, the original New Irish Farm Cemetery post, with photos taken in 2008, published in June 2011 as part of ‘The Road to Passchendaele’ series. To which I have naturally tagged this new post. So as we tour the cemetery,… …I’ll include a few shots from my first visit such as this one – they’ll be easy to spot, if I forget to mention them, as it was high summer at the time, the trees awash with green, and all the flowers in bloom, as you can see. You might well notice some apparent differences in the surrounding landscape as we continue.
